                 A five-list obstruction on an eleven-vertex tree
                                              Alec Kriebel
                                        Independent researcher
                                      ORCID: 0009-0001-9320-500X

                                   17 October 2026           Version 1.0


                                                Abstract
          We exhibit an eleven-vertex tree T with ordinary L(2, 1) initial-segment palette size 5 and
      arbitrary-list parameter 6. An explicit assignment of five-element positive-integer lists is in-
      feasible by a short forcing argument. An ordinary five-palette labeling and the known ∆ + 3
      tree list bound give the exact values. This contradicts the universal equality stated in Kohl’s
      2006 Conjecture 4 and dissertation Conjecture 4.4. Independent pendant-path extensions give
      infinitely many examples of unbounded diameter. Historical priority, minimal order and present
      openness are not claimed.


1    Conventions and the historical target
An L(2, 1)-labeling of a finite simple graph assigns positive integers to vertices so that adjacent
labels differ by at least 2, and labels at distance 2 differ. Write χ(2,1) (G) for the least k allowing such
                                                                            (2,1)
a labeling from the common initial segment [k] = {1, . . . , k}. Write χℓ (G) for the least k such that
every assignment of k-element subsets L(v) of the positive integers admits a labeling f (v) ∈ L(v).
Lists need not be intervals. Ordinary zero-based span λ(G) satisfies χ(2,1) (G) = λ(G) + 1.
    Kohl’s Oberwolfach contribution [1, Conjecture 4, p. 416] and dissertation [2, Conjecture 4.4,
                (2,1)
p. 124] state χℓ (T ) = χ(2,1) (T ) for every tree T . The example below is a full negative answer to
that stated universal equality. The identification is historical; it does not assert that the conjecture
remained open immediately before this work.


2    The obstruction
Let T have the path a − b − c − d − e. Attach leaves a1 , a2 to a, b1 to b, d1 to d, and e1 , e2 to e.
These are all vertices and edges, so T has eleven vertices, ten edges, maximum degree 3, radius 3,
and diameter 6. Set
                             A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5},   B = {1, 3, 4, 5, 6}.
Assign B to a1 , a2 , e1 , e2 and A to every other vertex.

Theorem 1. The displayed assignment has no L(2, 1)-labeling, while χ(2,1) (T ) = 5, or equivalently
                (2,1)
λ(T ) = 4, and χℓ (T ) = 6.

Proof. In a putative list labeling, the three neighbors of b all have list A and are pairwise at distance
2. If f (b) = 2, 3, 4, respectively, at most two elements of A differ from f (b) by at least 2. Thus
f (b) ∈ {1, 5}. The same argument applies to d. Since b, d are at distance 2, they receive different

                                                     1
endpoint labels. Reversing the spine and its attached leaves preserves the assignment, so assume
f (b) = 1 and f (d) = 5. Then f (c) = 3.
    The edge ab and the distance-two pair ac force f (a) ∈ {4, 5}. Each of a1 , a2 has list B, must
differ by at least 2 from f (a), and must avoid 1 = f (b). If f (a) = 4, only 6 remains; if f (a) = 5,
only 3 remains. In either case the two leaves receive the same label, although they are at distance
2. This contradiction proves infeasibility.
    An ordinary labeling from [5] is

                             v   a b c d e a 1 a 2 b1 d 1 e 1 e 2
                           f (v) 1 5 3 1 5 3 4 2 4 2 3

as checked directly on edges and pairs of neighbors. A degree-three vertex cannot be labeled from
[4]: each possible center label leaves at most two admissible neighbor labels, whereas its three
                                                                             (2,1)
neighbors must be distinct. Hence χ(2,1) (T ) = 5. The bad five-lists imply χℓ (T ) ≥ 6; Lemma 1
gives the reverse inequality.
                                                                        (2,1)
Lemma 1 (Known tree bound). For every nonempty finite tree S, χℓ                (S) ≤ ∆(S) + 3.

Proof. Root the tree and label in breadth-first order. For a nonroot vertex v, its parent is its
only earlier neighbor, excluding at most three integers from L(v). Earlier vertices at distance 2
are its grandparent, if present, and earlier siblings. There are at most ∆(S) − 1 of these: if the
parent is the root there is no grandparent, and otherwise the parent has at most ∆(S) − 1 children.
They exclude at most one label each. At most ∆(S) + 2 labels are therefore forbidden, leaving a
choice from any (∆(S) + 3)-element list. The root has no earlier constraints. This also covers a
singleton.
                                                               (d,s)
   For positive integers d ≥ s, the more general tree bound χℓ (S) ≤ s∆(S) + 2d − 1 is attributed
to Voigt in [1, p. 416 and reference 8 on p. 417], citing Kohl, Schreyer, Tuza and Voigt [3]. The
proof above is included for self-contained verification, without a novelty claim for the bound.


3   Infinitely many countertrees
Corollary 1. Attach one path, of any independently chosen nonnegative finite length, outward from
                                                                             (2,1)
each of the six leaves of T . Every resulting tree S has χ(2,1) (S) = 5 and χℓ (S) = 6. The family
has unbounded diameter.

Proof. The old tree is an induced subtree, its old distances are unchanged, and the maximum degree
remains 3. Extend the displayed ordinary labeling successively along each new path. The parent
excludes at most three labels of [5], and the grandparent at most one, so a choice always remains.
New vertices on different added paths have distance at least 4; no further constraints arise. Thus
χ(2,1) (S) ≤ 5, with the reverse inequality by restriction to T . Extend the infeasible lists on T by
arbitrary five-element lists on new vertices. Any labeling would restrict to a forbidden labeling of
         (2,1)                                     (2,1)
T , so χℓ (S) ≥ 6, while the tree bound gives χℓ (S) ≤ 6.


4   Verification, attribution and limitations
The proof is elementary and independent of computational search. The accompanying verification
archive contains the exact graph, lists and ordinary witness, TeX source, a standard-library Python


                                                  2
enumerator, expected results and byte manifests. Its exhaustive finite counts are 0, 8, 6336 for
common palettes [4], [5], [6], respectively, and 0 for the displayed five-lists. These computations
check fixed instances; the universal six-list bound and the entire infinite family follow from the
proofs, not from sampling. A separate construction-input reconstruction used different constraint
propagation and tree-state mechanisms, froze its results before comparison, and did not read the
candidate proof. The construction was supplied to it, so this is not an independent discovery claim.
Supplementary recurrence details include explicit local-state admissibility; the main obstruction
needs no recurrence.
     General-graph separations were known earlier. Fiala and Škrekovski’s 2001 preprint [4, Fig. 4,
p. 14] displays a ten-vertex cyclic graph with an ordinary five-palette labeling and infeasible five-
lists. That figure does not itself contradict tree equality. A bounded primary-source and citation
audit did not verify an earlier negative tree resolution. Relevant inaccessible or unlocated source
bodies remain, as recorded in the supporting priority audit. Accordingly this note makes no claim of
historical firstness, minimality, a new obstruction mechanism, or present openness. The inspected
2001 preprint is cited as such; its content is not silently identified with the differently titled 2005
journal version.
     AI tools were used extensively in the research, proof development, literature review, computa-
tion, verification and writing. The internal independent and adversarial checks were AI-assisted.
This preprint is unrefereed: no external human peer review or formal proof-assistant certification
is claimed.
